explainers.title: Hello and welcome to Global Perspectives
explainers.body:
Hello, and welcome to Global Perspectives at Ehel Academy. This subject is a little different from your other lessons. It is not about learning lots of facts by heart. Instead, it teaches you thinking skills that you can use all your life, in every subject and out in the real world.

There are six thinking skills in Global Perspectives. You will grow all of them, little by little, over your years here:

This whole unit is about the very first skill: Research. It is a lovely skill to start with, because you need it before all the others. You cannot analyse, judge or explain a topic well until you have found out about it first.

Why does this matter outside school? Think about the choices grown-ups make every day. A parent picking the best clinic for a sick child. A shopkeeper choosing what to sell. A community deciding where to dig a new well. All of them are really doing research. They ask questions, find information, decide who to trust, and choose. When you practise research now, you are learning to make good choices for the rest of your life.
bullets: Research — finding out about the world in a careful, tidy way.
Analysis — breaking a topic into parts and asking why things happen.
Evaluation — deciding how strong an idea or a piece of evidence really is.
Reflection — thinking about how you learn and how you change your mind.
Collaboration — working well together with other people.
Communication — sharing your ideas clearly so others understand.

explainers.title: How you will learn this unit
explainers.body:
You are learning in the Ehel Academy way. This means three kinds of help all work together:

In the old way of this subject, learners were told to 'talk to a partner' or 'talk as a class'. In our way, your AI tutor is your partner and your class. So every time you see an 'Ask Your AI Tutor' box, treat it like a real chat. Say your ideas out loud, or type them, and let your tutor help your thinking grow.
bullets: You, at your own speed. You read, think and do the activities in your own time. You can slow down on a hard part, or move quickly through an easy one.

Your AI tutor, ready any time, day or night. Whenever this book says 'Ask Your AI Tutor', you talk to your tutor like a friendly study partner. It will chat about your ideas, ask you questions, and help you at any hour.
Your teacher, about twice a week. In your live sessions you share your best work, ask your biggest questions, and get to know the other learners.

explainers.title: Meet Amara, our researcher
explainers.body:
To make each skill clear, we will follow one Year 5 learner through the whole unit. Her name is Amara, and she is a student at Ehel Academy in Hargeisa.

Hargeisa can get very hot and dry. One hot afternoon, Amara notices that many children at her school are thirsty. The water jug in her classroom is empty by the middle of the day, and some children have nothing to drink until they go home. Amara starts to wonder: do all the children at her school have enough clean water to drink on a hot day, and what would help?

That wonder becomes Amara's research project for this unit. As you meet each new skill, you will see exactly what Amara does with it. By the end, she will have real findings she can share. You will be doing the very same thing, with a topic that matters to you.

explainers.title: Your Challenge: your project for the whole unit
explainers.body:
This unit builds up to one project we call your Challenge. A Challenge is a topic that matters both in the world and right where you live. You will come back to it, lesson after lesson, and each new skill adds another piece.

Here are some topics that are big in the world and also real in the Horn of Africa. Any of these could be your Challenge:

Your friends care about different things. Karim is curious about litter. Yasmin wants more books in the school library. Sami wishes for more shade trees in the yard. Any of these could grow into a Challenge.

You do not have to choose right now. As you work through the skills, keep a note of any topic that makes you curious, or that makes you think 'someone should fix this'. Those feelings are a great sign of a good Challenge topic.
bullets: Clean water to drink at school or at home
Litter and plastic waste in our streets
Healthy food and good school snacks
Staying safe on busy roads
Trees and shade in the schoolyard
Solar lamps to help children study after dark
Looking after wildlife, like the sea turtles on the Berbera coast
Making sure every child, girls and boys, can stay in school

explainers.title: So what is research?
explainers.body:
Many people think research just means typing a question into a phone and reading the first answer. Real research is more careful than that. Research means finding out about something in a tidy, careful way, from more than one place, so that you can trust what you learn and explain it to others.

Good research usually follows a few simple steps:

You will learn every step in this unit. Notice that 'search on a phone' is only a small part of one step. Researchers also ask people, watch what happens with their own eyes, and read books.
bullets: Ask a clear question worth finding out about.
Think about where the answers might come from.
Find information from more than one place.
Check whether you can trust what you find.
Write the important parts in your own words.
Sort out what you found, and share it.

explainers.title: Start a research notebook
explainers.body:
Before you meet the first skill, start a simple habit that real researchers use: keep a research notebook. This can be any notebook where you write everything about your Challenge. Each time you work, write the date, then jot down what you did and what you found.

A research notebook helps you in three ways. It keeps all your notes in one place, so nothing gets lost. It shows how your ideas change over time. And it makes sharing your findings much easier later, because your work is already there. Keep your notebook next to you as you read on.

explainers.title: Skill 1: Ask lots of questions
explainers.body:
Every research project starts with questions. Before you pick one question to study, it helps to think of as many questions as you can. A great way to do this is a mind-map.

To make a mind-map, write your topic in the middle of a page and draw a circle around it. Then, all around it, write every question you can think of about the topic. Do not stop to judge them yet. Just get lots of questions out of your head and onto the page.

It also helps to sort your questions into groups. For a topic like water, some questions are about how we use it, and some are about problems it can cause.

explainers.title: Skill 2: What makes a good question?
explainers.body:
Some questions are more useful for research than others. Two ideas help you here: open and closed questions, and picking a question that is worth finding out about.

A closed question has a short answer, often just yes or no. An open question opens up a longer answer. Both can be useful, but open questions usually tell you more.

A good research question is also worth finding out about. It should not be so easy that you already know the answer, and not so huge that you could never finish. The best question is one you really want to answer, and one you can actually find out about.
bullets: Closed question: Do you drink water at school? The answer is just yes or no.
Open question: What stops you from drinking enough water at school? The answer can be a whole sentence.
Number question: How many cups of water do you drink at school? Numbers are easy to count and compare.

explainers.title: Skill 3: Find information in different places
explainers.body:
The places your information comes from are called sources. A source can be a book, a website, a map, a video, or a person. Good researchers know that different questions need different sources.

There are two easy ways to find information:

Strong research often uses both. Books and websites give you the big picture. Asking and watching tell you what is true right here, in your own school, which no book could know.
bullets: Find it out yourself. You can ask people questions, or watch with your own eyes. Asking the children in your class, or watching the water jug, are ways of finding out yourself.
Use what others have made. You can read a book, look at a map, or read a website that someone else has written.

explainers.title: Skill 4: Is this a good source?
explainers.body:
Not everything you read or hear is true or useful. Before you use a source, stop and check it. You can ask three simple questions: Who made it? Is it about my question? Can I trust it?

A source can be very useful, possibly useful, or not useful. A good researcher keeps the useful ones and lets the others go, even if they were easy to find.
bullets: Who made it? A person who really knows the topic is easier to trust.
Is it about my question? A source can be interesting but still not help your question. You want one that fits.
Can I trust it? Does it give real facts? Do other good sources say the same thing?

explainers.title: Skill 5: Make a prediction and a questionnaire
explainers.body:
When you find things out for yourself, it helps to start with a prediction. A prediction is a smart guess about what you think you will find. Later, your research will show if your guess was right.

One great tool for finding out is a questionnaire. This is a set of the same questions that you ask many people. When lots of people answer the same questions, you can count and compare the answers.

explainers.title: Skill 6: Do your research and check your guess
explainers.body:
Now you carry out your research. You ask your questionnaire questions, or you watch and record what happens. This part is exciting, because you find out something no book could tell you about your own school.

Be kind and polite when you ask people. Let them say no if they want to, and always say thank you. Good researchers respect the people who help them.

When you finish, look back at your prediction. Was your guess completely right, mostly right, partly right, or not right? Being wrong is not a problem at all. Finding out the real answer is the whole point of research.

explainers.title: Skill 7: Take notes in your own words
explainers.body:
When you read a book or website, you do not copy it. You take notes. Notes are short reminders of the important ideas, written in your own words. Writing in your own words shows that you really understood.

Two tips help you take good notes:
bullets: Write only the parts that answer your question. You do not need the rest.
Keep notes short. Use quick words instead of full sentences, and even short forms, like writing 'BW' for 'bottled water'.

explainers.title: Skill 8: Record and share what you found
explainers.body:
Your findings are only useful if others can understand them. So you need to record them tidily and share them clearly. A pile of answers means nothing until you sort it out.

A table or a tally chart is a great way to record answers. Then you can show your findings in the clearest way for other people. You might pick:

How you share depends on what you found and who you are sharing with. Numbers often look best in a chart. A person's story often looks best in a few careful words.
bullets: A table, to lay out your answers in rows.
A tally chart, to count how many people gave each answer.
A bar chart, to show numbers so the pattern is easy to see.
A few words or pictures, to share a person's story.

explainers.title: Staying safe and being fair
explainers.body:
Because research means going out into the world and online, a good researcher also learns to stay safe and to be fair. These are part of the skill, not extra rules.

Staying safe online. When you look things up online, keep yourself safe:

Being fair. Global Perspectives is about seeing a topic from many sides. On almost any topic, people think different things, and a fair researcher listens to everyone before deciding.
bullets: Never share your full name, home address, school, or photos with strangers online.
If a page asks you to sign up, download something, or 'click to win', stop and check with a trusted adult.
If a page upsets or worries you, close it and tell your teacher or a grown-up at home.

explainers.title: Amara's whole journey
explainers.body:
You have now met every research skill in this unit. Here is how Amara used them, one after another, to turn a small worry into real findings:

By following these steps, Amara turned an everyday worry about thirsty children into real, tidy findings she can share with her teacher and her school. In the Activities file, you will do the very same thing with your own Challenge, one small step at a time, with your AI tutor beside you.
bullets: She made a mind-map of lots of questions about water at school.
She picked one good question that was worth finding out about.
She thought about the best sources: asking children, and checking where the school water comes from.
She checked that her sources were useful and could be trusted.
She made a prediction and wrote a simple questionnaire.
She asked 20 children, then checked if her guess was right.
She took notes in her own words, and put her answers in a table.
She drew a bar chart and shared what she found.

explainers.title: What comes next
explainers.body: The next unit is Analysis. Once you can research a topic well, analysis helps you look closely and ask why things happen and who is affected. Strong research now will make analysis much easier later. Well done for starting your Global Perspectives journey with a strong first step.

bigIdeas.title: One big idea to remember
lines: In Global Perspectives, the topic is like a boat. The skill is where the boat takes you.
We will use real topics such as water, litter and school meals.
But the real prize is not to become an expert on water. It is to become a good researcher who could find out about almost anything.

bigIdeas.title: A quick clue from a website address
lines: An address ending in .gov is often an official government site, and is usually careful and reliable.
An address ending in .org is often a helping organisation, and can be a good source.
If lots of people can change a page, like some wiki or social media pages, take care. It may not be correct.
These are only clues, not proof. Always check who made it and whether other sources agree.

bigIdeas.title: What makes a good questionnaire question
lines: It is clear and easy to understand.
It is about your topic.
It can be answered quickly.
It does not push people to one answer. Do you agree our water is terrible? is a pushy question. How would you describe our water? is fair.

bigIdeas.title: What a good note is like
lines: It is short, just a few words, not a whole paragraph.
It is in your own words, never copied word for word.
It keeps only what answers your question.
It says which book or website it came from, so you can find it again.

bigIdeas.title: Being fair to different people
lines: People live in different ways and believe different things, and that is a good thing to notice.
For example, some families celebrate Eid, and some families celebrate Christmas. A fair researcher asking about school holidays would listen to both, evenly.
Being fair does not mean having no opinion. It means you listen to many people first, then make up your mind.

bigIdeas.title: Quick clues from a website address
lines: Ends in .gov: often an official government site, usually reliable.
Ends in .org: often a helping organisation, often a good source.
Lots of people can change it, like some wiki or social media pages: take care and check elsewhere.
Clues are not proof. Always check who made it.

bigIdeas.title: Your three golden rules
lines: Ask a clear question that you really want to answer.
Use more than one source, and check that you can trust them.
Write in your own words, and keep it tidy so you can share it.

bigIdeas.title: Your Challenge runs through everything
lines: Pick one topic that matters where you live. This is your Challenge.
You will build on it in every activity, so choose something you really care about.
By the end you will have real research you can share with your teacher.

bigIdeas.title: Two sources about clean water
lines: Source 1: A page on a health group's .org site, written by a named doctor, updated this year.
Source 2: A post with no name and no date, that says our water is the worst in the whole world.

bigIdeas.title: Check each question
lines: Is it clear and easy to understand?
Is it about my topic?
Can it be answered quickly?
Is it fair, and not pushy? Change any question that pushes people to one answer.

bigIdeas.title: Source passage: Water on a hot day
lines: On very hot days, our bodies lose a lot of water when we sweat. If we do not drink enough, we feel tired and find it hard to think.
Children need to drink water all through the school day, not just at home. A cool, clean water point at school helps everyone stay well and learn better.

models.title: Research happens at home too
lines: Imagine you want to buy the sweetest mangoes at the market.
You ask a clear question: which seller has the sweetest mangoes for the best price?
You find information: you smell the fruit, ask the seller, and ask a friend who bought some yesterday.
You check who to trust: the seller wants a sale, so you trust your friend a bit more.
Then you choose. That is real research, and you already do it.

So research is not a strange school-only thing. It is a careful, honest way of finding things out, and you can get better and better at it. In this unit you will simply learn to do it on purpose, with more skill.

models.title: Amara's mind-map about water at school
lines: In the middle Amara writes: drinking water at my school.
Some questions are about use: When do children get thirsty? How much water do we drink in a day?
Some are about problems: Why does the jug run out? Where does our school water come from? Is it clean?
A messy mind-map with lots of questions is much better than a tidy one with only two.

models.title: Amara chooses her question
lines: Too easy: Is water good for you? Amara already knows the answer is yes.
Too huge: What is water? That would take years to answer.
Just right: How can we make sure every child at Ehel Academy has enough clean water on a hot day?
It is clear, it is about her own school, and she can really find out about it.

models.title: Sana matches a question to a source
lines: Sana wants to know where her town's water comes from. A map or the water office can tell her.
She also wants to know how much water children drink at school. No book knows that, so she asks the children herself.
Different questions, different sources. Sana picks the source that fits each question.

models.title: Idris and the sea turtles on the Berbera coast
lines: Idris finds two pages about sea turtles near Berbera.
One is on a wildlife group's .org site, written by named scientists, and updated this year.
The other is a post with no name and no date.
Idris trusts the first one much more, and looks for a second good source to check it.

models.title: Amara's prediction and questionnaire
lines: Amara's prediction: I think most children finish their water before lunch on a hot day.
Her questionnaire asks each child: How many cups of water did you drink today? Did you run out? When?
She will ask many children in her class, so she can count the answers.

models.title: What Amara found
lines: Amara asked 20 children in her class.
She found that 14 of them ran out of water before lunch on a hot day.
Her prediction, that most children finish their water before lunch, turned out to be mostly right.
Now she has a real fact she can share.

models.title: Karim's notes about litter
lines: Karim reads: Plastic bags are cheap and useful for a few minutes, but most are thrown away the same day and blow into the street.
His note says: plastic bags used once, then thrown away, end up in streets.
It is shorter, in his own words, and keeps only the main idea.

models.title: How Amara shares her findings
lines: Amara puts her answers in a table: cups of water drunk, and who ran out.
Then she draws a simple bar chart to show that 14 of 20 children ran out before lunch.
The chart makes the problem easy to see in one glance, so her teacher understands it fast.

models.title: A model, in case you get stuck
lines: Topic: drinking water at my school.
Research question: How can we make sure every child at Ehel Academy has enough clean water on a hot day?
It is clear, it is about my own school, and I can really find out about it.

models.title: Copying versus your own words
lines: The passage says: our bodies lose a lot of water when we sweat.
A copied note just repeats those exact words, which we do not do.
A good note in your own words might be: we lose water by sweating in the heat.

models.title: A model: Amara shares her findings
lines: Finding: 14 of the 20 children she asked ran out of water before lunch.
Best way to show it: a simple bar chart, because it is numbers and a chart shows the pattern fast.
Amara's teacher can see the problem in one glance.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Say hello to your AI tutor. Tell it: I am starting Unit 1 of Global Perspectives, and the skill is Research.
Ask it: In one or two easy sentences, why is research a useful skill, even outside school?
Then tell your tutor which of the six skills you think will be the most fun for you, and why.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor, in your own words, what you think research means now.
Ask it: Is my idea missing anything important?
Then ask your tutor to give you one everyday example of research that has nothing to do with school.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your topic. Ask it to help you think of eight or more questions about it.
Then sort your questions into two groups: questions about uses, and questions about problems.
Ask your tutor to suggest one interesting question you did not think of.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Write two questions about your topic: one closed and one open.
Read them to your AI tutor and ask which one would tell you more, and why.
Then ask your tutor to help you pick one good research question that is worth finding out about.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor one question from your topic.
Ask it to help you list two places you could find the answer: one book or website, and one person you could ask.
Then ask: which source would be best for this question, and why?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about one source you found: who made it, and where it is from.
Ask your tutor to help you decide if it is useful and if you can trust it.
Ask: what is one more thing I should check before I use this source?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor a prediction about your topic. Start with the words: I think.
Ask it to help you write three or four clear questionnaire questions.
Then ask: are any of my questions pushy or unclear, and how can I fix them?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor what you found out when you did your research.
Ask it: was my prediction completely, mostly, partly, or not right?
Ask your tutor what surprised you, and what you could find out next.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read a short bit about your topic, then write two or three notes in your own words.
Read your notes to your AI tutor and ask: have I copied any words, or is this really in my own words?
Ask your tutor if you missed the main idea.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor what kind of information you gathered: numbers, or people's stories.
Ask it to suggest the clearest way to show your findings.
Ask your tutor to check that your table or chart is easy to understand.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your Challenge topic.
Ask it to help you think of someone who might see your topic differently from you.
Ask: how can I be fair to people who do not agree with me?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your topic and your two reasons.
Ask it: is this topic a good size for a Year 5 project, or is it too big?
Ask your tutor for one way to make the topic more about your own school or town.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your mind-map questions to your AI tutor.
Ask it which two or three questions look the most interesting, and why.
Ask your tutor to add one good question you did not think of.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your answers to your AI tutor and ask it to check them.
Ask: which of my two new questions would tell me more, and why?
Ask your tutor to help you turn a closed question into an open one.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Give your AI tutor your research question.
Ask: is it clear, worth finding out about, and possible to answer? Where is it weakest?
Ask your tutor to help you make it better.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your four pairs to your AI tutor and ask it to check them.
Ask it to explain any you got wrong, in an easy way.
Ask: for my own topic, would I mostly ask people, or mostly look in books and websites?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor which source you trust more and why.
Ask it to check your three checking questions.
Ask your tutor to help you decide if your real source is useful and can be trusted.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your prediction and four questions to your AI tutor.
Ask it: are any of my questions pushy or unclear? How would you fix them?
Ask your tutor whether my questions will really test my prediction.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your notes to your AI tutor.
Ask it: have I copied any words, or is this really in my own words?
Ask your tutor if I found the true main idea.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor what you found and who you want to share it with.
Ask it to suggest the clearest way to show your findings.
Ask your tutor to check that your draft is easy to understand.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your three Challenge sentences to your AI tutor.
Ask it: from what I found, what is one good next question I could research?
Ask your tutor to help you plan your very next research step.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your fixed questions to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your new questions are open and fair, and not pushy.
Ask your tutor to show you one more way to fix any question you found hard.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your four answers to your AI tutor.
Ask it which answer was strongest and why.
Ask your tutor for one more short story like these to try.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your reflection answers to your AI tutor.
Ask it to help you notice how your thinking changed from the start of the unit to now.
Ask your tutor which research skill to work on next, and why.

speakingPrompts.title: Ask someone at home
lines: Ask a grown-up at home which problem in your area they most wish someone would solve.
Write down their answer, and bring it to your next teacher session.
What the adults around you care about can point you to a great Challenge topic.

speakingPrompts.title: Bring it to your teacher
lines: Save your final research question.
Share it in your next teacher session and ask if it is a good fit for your topic.

speakingPrompts.title: A real-world step
lines: With a grown-up's help, ask your questions to a few people at home or at school.
Bring what you find to your next teacher session, and compare it with your prediction.

toolkit.title: The research steps at a glance
toolkit.intro: Whatever your topic, good research follows the same simple steps. Come back to this list whenever you feel stuck.
items: Ask a clear question worth finding out about.
Think about where the answers could come from.
Find information from more than one place.
Check whether you can trust what you find.
Write the important parts in your own words.
Share what you found in a clear way.

toolkit.title: What research means, in plain words
toolkit.intro:
Research means finding out about something in a careful, tidy way, from more than one place, so that you can trust what you learn and explain it to someone else. It is not just typing a question into a phone.

Two habits sit at the heart of it. First, always use more than one place, because one source can be wrong. Second, always write in your own words. If you remember nothing else, remember those two habits.

toolkit.title: Cambridge Stage 5 Research goals
toolkit.intro: Global Perspectives sets out what good research looks like at this stage. Here are the four Research goals, in child-friendly words. Your teacher may talk about these numbers.

rows: Think of good questions, and pick one that is worth finding out about.
Find useful sources, decide if you can trust them, and take notes in your own words.
Make a prediction, and use a questionnaire, an interview or watching to test it.
Sort your answers and show them clearly, in a table, a chart or a picture.
Gives a short answer, often just yes or no.
Do you drink water at school?
What stops you from drinking enough water?
Asks for a number you can count.
How many cups of water do you drink?

toolkit.title: Choosing where to find information
toolkit.intro: Pick the source that fits your question. Some questions you answer by asking people or watching. Some you answer with a book, a map or a website.

rows: You want what people here think or do.
How many children run out of water?
You want to see what really happens.
Does the water jug run out before lunch?
You want facts others have already found.
Where does our town's water come from?

toolkit.title: Template: Taking notes from a source
toolkit.intro: Copy this table for each source. Keep notes short, in your own words, and only what answers your question.

toolkit.title: Ways to show your findings
toolkit.intro: Pick the way that makes your findings easiest to understand.

rows: Laying out your answers in rows.
Counting how many people gave each answer.
Showing numbers so the pattern is easy to see.
A few words or a picture

toolkit.title: Sentence starters for sharing findings
toolkit.intro: Use these to share what you found:
items: The topic I researched is ...
My question was ...
I found out that ...
Most people said ...
I was surprised that ...
So I now think ...

toolkit.title: Question starters for questionnaires and interviews
toolkit.intro:
Use these to write clear, fair questions. Keep them short and never pushy.

Do not start with 'Don't you agree ...?' or 'Isn't it obvious ...?'. These are pushy and point people to one answer.
items: How often do you ...?
How many ...?
What do you think about ...?
What would help you most with ...?
Can you tell me about a time when ...? (good for interviews)

toolkit.title: One last thing to remember
toolkit.intro: Every good researcher started exactly where you are now. You do not have to be perfect. You just have to be careful, honest and curious. If you get stuck, that is normal, and your AI tutor is ready to help you at any time.

checklists.title: Checklist: Is this a good question?
checklists.intro: Tick each one. If you cannot tick them all, change your question.
items: Clear — anyone would understand what I am asking.
Worth it — it is not so easy that I already know the answer.
Not too big — I could actually finish it.
Cared about — it matters to me and to other people.
Findable — I can really find the answer.

checklists.title: Checklist: Can I trust this source?
checklists.intro: Ask these three questions about every source before you use it.
items: Who made it, and do they know the topic?
Is it about my question, or just interesting?
Can I trust it? Does it give real facts, and do other good sources agree?

challenge.intro: Look back at the topic list in the Lesson file: clean water, litter, healthy food, road safety, trees and shade, solar lamps, wildlife, staying in school. Pick one that matters in your area, or think of your own. The best topic is one you are really curious about, because you will work on it for the whole unit.
topics: Write your topic in one sentence: The topic I am working on is ...
Write one reason you care about it.
Write one reason other people in your area might care too.
checkpoints: I was surprised to find out that ...

activities.title: Mind-map your questions
activities.label: Activity 2: Mind-map your questions
activities.intro:
Before you pick a research question, you need lots of questions to choose from. A mind-map helps you get them all out of your head.

Try to think of some questions about how things are used, and some about problems. A messy map with many questions is exactly what you want.
steps: Write your topic in the middle of a page and draw a circle around it.
Around it, write as many questions as you can, at least eight. Do not judge them yet.
Draw a line to join any questions that go together.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your mind-map questions to your AI tutor.
Ask it which two or three questions look the most interesting, and why.
Ask your tutor to add one good question you did not think of.

activities.title: Sort open and closed questions
activities.label: Activity 3: Sort open and closed questions
activities.intro:
Remember, a closed question has a short yes or no answer, and an open question opens up a longer one. Look at these four questions. For each one, write open or closed.

Then write one open question and one closed question about your own topic.
steps: A. Do you drink water at school?
B. What stops you from drinking enough water?
C. Is there litter in our schoolyard?
D. What could our school do about litter?

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your answers to your AI tutor and ask it to check them.
Ask: which of my two new questions would tell me more, and why?
Ask your tutor to help you turn a closed question into an open one.

activities.title: Pick and check your research question
activities.label: Activity 4: Pick and check your research question
activities.intro: Now choose the one question you want to research for your Challenge. Take your time. It is fine to write a question, decide it is not quite right, and change it. That reworking is part of the skill, not a mistake.
steps: Write down what you most want to find out about your topic.
Write three questions about it.
Pick the one you like best, or join two together into one.
Check it: is it clear? Is it worth finding out about? Can you really find the answer? Change it until you can say yes to all three.

boxes.title: A model, in case you get stuck
lines: Topic: drinking water at my school.
Research question: How can we make sure every child at Ehel Academy has enough clean water on a hot day?
It is clear, it is about my own school, and I can really find out about it.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Give your AI tutor your research question.
Ask: is it clear, worth finding out about, and possible to answer? Where is it weakest?
Ask your tutor to help you make it better.

boxes.title: Bring it to your teacher
lines: Save your final research question.
Share it in your next teacher session and ask if it is a good fit for your topic.

activities.title: Match questions to sources
activities.label: Activity 5: Match questions to sources
activities.intro:
Different questions need different sources. Match each question (1 to 4) to the best source (A to D).

Write the pairs, like 1-C. Then write one sentence: why does a good source depend on the question you are asking?
steps: Where does our town's water come from?
How many children run out of water at school?
How do sea turtles live on the coast?
How much does bottled water cost in the market?
A. Ask many children at school.
B. A wildlife website or book.
C. A map or the water office.
D. Ask a market seller.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your four pairs to your AI tutor and ask it to check them.
Ask it to explain any you got wrong, in an easy way.
Ask: for my own topic, would I mostly ask people, or mostly look in books and websites?

activities.title: Is this a good source?
activities.label: Activity 6: Is this a good source?
activities.intro: For your own topic, you need sources you can trust. Judge these two sources for a topic about clean water.
steps: Which source would you trust more? Write one reason why.
Write the three checking questions you can ask about any source.
Now think of one real source for your own topic, and check it with those three questions.

boxes.title: Two sources about clean water
lines: Source 1: A page on a health group's .org site, written by a named doctor, updated this year.
Source 2: A post with no name and no date, that says our water is the worst in the whole world.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor which source you trust more and why.
Ask it to check your three checking questions.
Ask your tutor to help you decide if your real source is useful and can be trusted.

activities.title: Make a prediction and a questionnaire
activities.label: Activity 7: Make a prediction and a questionnaire
activities.intro: Now plan some research you do yourself. First make a prediction, then write a questionnaire to test it.
steps: Write a prediction about your topic. Start with I think ...
Write four clear questions to ask many people.
Decide who you will ask, and how many people.

boxes.title: Check each question
lines: Is it clear and easy to understand?
Is it about my topic?
Can it be answered quickly?
Is it fair, and not pushy? Change any question that pushes people to one answer.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your prediction and four questions to your AI tutor.
Ask it: are any of my questions pushy or unclear? How would you fix them?
Ask your tutor whether my questions will really test my prediction.

boxes.title: A real-world step
lines: With a grown-up's help, ask your questions to a few people at home or at school.
Bring what you find to your next teacher session, and compare it with your prediction.

activities.title: Take notes in your own words
activities.label: Activity 8: Take notes in your own words
activities.intro: Read the short passage below. It is your source for this task. Take notes in your own words, then check them.
steps: Write the main idea of the passage in one sentence, in your own words.
Write two short notes, in your own words, about why water matters on a hot day.
Write down where these notes came from (this passage).

boxes.title: Source passage: Water on a hot day
lines: On very hot days, our bodies lose a lot of water when we sweat. If we do not drink enough, we feel tired and find it hard to think.
Children need to drink water all through the school day, not just at home. A cool, clean water point at school helps everyone stay well and learn better.

boxes.title: Copying versus your own words
lines: The passage says: our bodies lose a lot of water when we sweat.
A copied note just repeats those exact words, which we do not do.
A good note in your own words might be: we lose water by sweating in the heat.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your notes to your AI tutor.
Ask it: have I copied any words, or is this really in my own words?
Ask your tutor if I found the true main idea.

activities.title: Do your research and share it
activities.label: Activity 9: Do your research and share it
activities.intro: Time to gather your information and share it clearly. If you can, ask your questionnaire to a few people. If not, write the answers you think you would get, and show how you would share them.
steps: Write down your findings so far, in short points.
Put your answers in a table or a tally chart.
Choose the clearest way to show them: a table, a bar chart, or a few words telling a person's story.
Make a first draft of your chosen way, and write one sentence saying why it suits your findings.

boxes.title: A model: Amara shares her findings
lines: Finding: 14 of the 20 children she asked ran out of water before lunch.
Best way to show it: a simple bar chart, because it is numbers and a chart shows the pattern fast.
Amara's teacher can see the problem in one glance.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor what you found and who you want to share it with.
Ask it to suggest the clearest way to show your findings.
Ask your tutor to check that your draft is easy to understand.

practice.intro: Answer these in your notebook or out loud with your AI tutor. There are 12 questions. Do not worry if some are tricky; that is how you find out what to practise next. Try every question before you look at the answer key, and use your own words.
practice.prompt: In your own words, what does the word 'research' mean?
practice.answer: Research means finding out about something in a careful, tidy way, from more than one place, so you can trust it and explain it. (Any answer with this idea is right.)

practice.prompt: A mind-map helps you think of lots of ______ about your topic.
practice.answer: Questions.

practice.prompt: Is this open or closed: 'Do you drink water at school?'
practice.answer: Closed (the answer is just yes or no).

practice.prompt: Is this open or closed: 'What stops you from drinking enough water?'
practice.answer: Open (it opens up a longer answer).

practice.prompt: A smart guess about what you will find is called a ______.
practice.answer: Prediction.

practice.prompt: A set of the same questions you ask many people is called a ______.
practice.answer: Questionnaire.

practice.prompt: Name one thing that makes a source easy to trust.
practice.answer: Any one of: a named writer who knows the topic; it gives real facts; other good sources agree; it is up to date.

practice.prompt: A website address ending in ______ is often an official government site.
practice.answer: .gov (an official government site).

practice.prompt: When you take notes, should you copy word for word, or use your own words?
practice.answer: Use your own words.

practice.prompt: You want to know how many children run out of water at your school. Should you ask many children, or read a book?
practice.answer: Ask many children (no book knows how many children at your school run out of water).

practice.prompt: Name one clear way to show number findings so the pattern is easy to see.
practice.answer: A bar chart (or a tally chart).

practice.prompt: A question that pushes someone to one answer, like 'Don't you agree our water is terrible?', is called a ______ question.
practice.answer: A pushy question (also called a leading question).

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.intro: Match each research word (1 to 6) to the correct meaning (A to F). Write the pairs, like 1-C.
practice.prompt: Source
options: A. A smart guess about what you will find.
B. Short reminders of ideas, written in your own words.
C. A place your information comes from, like a book or a person.
D. A drawing of lots of questions around a topic.
E. A set of the same questions you ask many people.
F. A chart where you make a mark to count each answer.
practice.answer: C — A place your information comes from, like a book or a person.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Prediction
practice.answer: A — A smart guess about what you will find.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Questionnaire
practice.answer: E — A set of the same questions you ask many people.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Notes
practice.answer: B — Short reminders of ideas, written in your own words.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Mind-map
practice.answer: D — A drawing of lots of questions around a topic.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Tally chart
practice.answer: F — A chart where you make a mark to count each answer.

practice.intro: These short stories ask you to use what you have learned. Write a sentence or two for each.
practice.prompt: Leila wants to know what drivers really do at a busy road in Mogadishu. Should she watch the road herself, or read a book? Why?
practice.answer: She should watch the road herself, because she wants to see what drivers really do. Watching with your own eyes is the best way here.

practice.prompt: Omar finds two websites about solar lamps. One names its writers and is from this year. The other has no name and no date. Which should he trust more, and why?
practice.answer: The website with named writers, from this year, because you can see who made it and when.

practice.prompt: Nadia asks 20 children how many cups of water they drink. What is a clear way to show her numbers so the pattern is easy to see?
practice.answer: A bar chart, because it shows numbers so the pattern is easy to see.

practice.prompt: Idris reads a great fact but forgets to write down which website it came from. What problem will he have later?
practice.answer: He cannot say where the fact came from, so he cannot check it or find it again. He should have written down the source straight away.

reflection.prompt: Working on my own, at my own speed ...
Working with my AI tutor, my partner ...
Working with my teacher in live sessions ...
Writing in my research notebook as I went ...

vocabulary.meaning: Finding out about something in a tidy way, from more than one place.
The main question that guides your whole project.
A drawing of lots of questions around a topic.
A question that opens up a longer answer.
A question with a short answer, often just yes or no.
A place your information comes from: a person, book, website or map.
A set of the same questions you ask many people.
Asking one person questions to learn what they think.
Watching carefully and writing down what happens.
A smart guess about what you will find.
A question that unfairly points someone to one answer (also called a leading question).
The most important point of what you read.
Short reminders of the important ideas, written in your own words.
A chart where you make a mark to count each answer.
A chart that shows numbers as bars, so the pattern is easy to see.
A source is useful if it helps answer your question.
Able to be trusted; a reliable source is likely to be correct.
Being fair means listening to many people before you decide.
Something that can be checked and shown to be true.
What someone thinks or believes, which others may disagree with.
A notebook where you write your research as you go.

mistakes: Picking a question that is too easy, or far too big.
Trusting a website without checking who made it.
Copying words instead of writing notes in your own words.
Forgetting to write down where a fact came from.
Writing a pushy question that points people to one answer.
Gathering lots of answers but never sorting them out.

selfAssessment.statement: I can think of lots of questions about a topic.
I can tell an open question from a closed one.
I can pick a good research question worth finding out about.
I can find the right source for a question.
I can decide if a source is useful and can be trusted.
